newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico reserves, net assets rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico reserves, net assets rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said on Tuesday its international reserves as of June 6 were $22.287 billion, compared to $22.262 billion on May 30.
The central bank said that its net international assets as of the same date rose to $14.943 billion from $14.442 billion the week before.
The central bank said the increase of $501 million in net international assets during the period was due to:
--Net income for deposits of foreign currency by the federal government worth $48 million.
--Net income from operations with state oil company Pemex worth $492 million.

--A net loss of $39 million for a combination of factors including changes in the dollar value of non-dollar assets and liabilities held by the bank; net returns on interest rates and from trading of metals and securities; and changes in the net balances in dollar accounts of commercial banks at the central bank.
Banco de Mexico said that between May 30 and June 6 the monetary base fell 1.496 billion pesos due to a fall in the demand of bills and coins.
In the same period, the government's balance at the central bank fell 4.339 billion pesos. The balance of deposits belonging to bank insurance fund Fobaproa fell 3.665 billion pesos.

To offset the increase in liquidity that would have resulted from the drop in government and Fobaproa deposits, the central bank sold government paper worth 11.076 billion pesos, of which 2.447 billion pesos were direct and 8.559 billion pesos were via repurchase agreements.
The following table details Banco de Mexico's reserves and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.
May 30 June 6
International Reserves
U.S. Dollars $22.262 bln $22.287 bln
Monetary Base 80.684 79.188
Net International Assets*
U.S. Dollars $14.442 bln $14.943 bln
Net Domestic Credit -33.647 -40.159
*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
((--Henry Tricks, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7902))
